name: Oligopeptide-34

lead: Oligopeptide-34 is a cosmetic peptide used in brightening products. People use it to help even out skin tone and fade the appearance of pigmented spots.
It is found in professional and retail serums aimed at hyperpigmentation.

paras: It is described as reducing tyrosinase activity and melanin synthesis in melanocytes and limiting melanosome transfer to skin cells.
It is a topical cosmetic ingredient. Reported efficacy figures come from company-run tests, and no independent human trials were found.

chain: Reduces tyrosinase activity and melanosome transfer
angle.text: Applied topically in brightening serums, Oligopeptide-34 is used to fade the appearance of pigmented spots and even out complexion.

lead: Oligopeptide-34 is a synthetic 13-amino-acid peptide used in skin-brightening cosmetics. People use serums containing it to help fade the look of dark spots and even out skin tone, so skin looks clearer and more uniform.[1]

It is described as acting on pigment cells: it reduces melanin synthesis and tyrosinase activity in melanocytes and lowers the transfer of melanosomes (packets of melanin) to surrounding keratinocytes.[1] The International Dermal Institute says it was developed with an Asian biopharmaceutical company specialising in growth-factor-mimicking peptides, and positions it as a non-hydroquinone option for professional skin therapists treating hyperpigmentation.[1]
Published information consists largely of supplier and brand-reported tests; no independent peer-reviewed human trial of the ingredient was found.[1]
infobox: Reduces melanin synthesis and melanosome transfer
An Asian biopharmaceutical company specialising in growth-factor-mimicking peptides[1]

paras: Oligopeptide-34 is formulated into topical brightening products intended to address uneven tone and pigmented spots.[1]
Per the International Dermal Institute, the peptide reduces melanin synthesis and tyrosinase activity in melanocytes and reduces the transfer of melanosomes to keratinocytes.[1]

No independent published clinical studies found. The International Dermal Institute, which promotes the ingredient, reports company-conducted results: in human melanocytes stimulated with melanocyte-stimulating hormone, melanin fell by about 33 percent after 72 hours and tyrosinase activity dropped by 65 percent at the optimum concentration; in a comparison, pigmentation fell 47 percent with the peptide versus 27 percent for vitamin C and 40 percent for arbutin.[1] It also reports a twice-daily study of 22 Asian participants showing a statistically significant brightening effect on pigmented spots by spectrophotometer and subjective assessment, with 84 percent of panelists rating performance good or very good after eight weeks.[1] The page does not provide the underlying data or methods.[1]
